archetype.name: Super Bowl Contender (takeaway-fueled, balanced)
archetype.definition: A team whose efficiency on both sides of the ball ranks near the top of the league, with a ball-hawking defense turning good play into lopsided scores.

report.headline: Last year's lucky 13 wins have turned into a genuinely dominant team
report.take:
Jacksonville has the league's best point differential per game (13.5), the second-best net EPA, a top-five offense and a top-three defense by EPA. Its only two losses came by a touchdown at Denver and by three in a shootout with Houston. This is not a record built on close escapes. Its 0.85 wins over expected is modest, and the point differential alone implies 5.2 wins, so 6-2 is about what this team has earned.

History matters here. Last year's 13-4 team led the league in wins over expected (3.87) on a net EPA of 0.117, which was good but carried by luck. This year net EPA sits at 0.222 with far less help from close games. In Liam Coen's second year the underlying team has caught up to, and passed, last year's record. Trevor Lawrence has started every game and the passing offense is fifth in EPA. The run game is eighth in EPA even though the backs get only 1.81 yards before contact (30th), so Bhayshul Tuten and company are making something out of crowded fronts.

The numbers do flatter the scoreboard. The offense is only 13th in yards per game but fourth in scoring. The defense is 10th in yards allowed but second in points allowed. A league-best turnover margin of +1.1 a game, on 15 takeaways, explains that gap: short fields on offense and drives killed on defense. Some of that is real, since the pressure rate (seventh) and a league-best short-pass defense create mistakes. Takeaway rates still drift, and when they do this looks like a very good team rather than a 40-point juggernaut. The other soft spot is deep coverage, which ranks 27th in EPA. Cincinnati threw for 428 yards and Houston for 312, both through the air.

With a three-game division lead and a healthy roster, the AFC South is close to settled. The real tests are the road games at the Giants and Bears and a home date with Pittsburgh. Those three will show whether this defense holds up when takeaways don't arrive and a good quarterback goes over the top.

strengths.title: Elite efficiency on both sides
strengths.body: Jacksonville ranks fifth in offensive EPA and third in defensive EPA allowed, which adds up to the league's second-best net EPA and its best point differential per game. That balance is the most durable thing about the team, because it doesn't depend on one unit carrying the other. Even with some regression, the gap between this group and most of the schedule is wide.

strengths.title: A short-pass defense that forces mistakes
strengths.body: No defense in the league allows less EPA on short throws. Paired with the seventh-best pressure rate, that rush-and-rally style squeezes quarterbacks into bad decisions, which is where most of the 15 takeaways come from. The process looks repeatable. The exact takeaway count probably isn't.

strengths.title: Backs win where the line doesn't
strengths.body: The line gives runners almost nothing before contact, ranking 30th, yet the run game is sixth in stuff rate and eighth in EPA. It converts 90% of short-yardage tries, second in the league. Tuten's volume and decisiveness are carrying the ground game, which keeps Lawrence in manageable downs.

concerns.title: Scoring leans on the turnover margin
concerns.body: A league-best +9 turnover differential is the bridge between middling yardage ranks and elite scoring ranks. Takeaway luck tends to cool over a season. When it does, expect fewer 35-point games and more one-score contests like the ones against Cincinnati and Philadelphia. This is the clearest regression candidate on the card.

concerns.title: Vulnerable over the top
concerns.body: The defense allows the sixth-worst EPA on deep passes, and slot or third receivers have found room: WR3 production over average ranks 31st. That is the cost of a scheme built to smother the short game. Quarterbacks willing to push the ball, like Cincinnati's 428-yard day, are the profile that beats it.

concerns.title: Line penalties and a slow clock
concerns.body: The offensive line draws 4.1 penalties a game, sixth-worst, and Lawrence's time to throw ranks 23rd. Flags put drives behind schedule: there were 125 penalty yards at Cincinnati and 100 against Philadelphia, both close games. Against a good pass rush this is the most likely way the offense stalls.

trend.note: Early blowouts gave way to a tight middle stretch of two-point and five-point wins and the shootout loss to Houston. The last two games, 42-7 over Indianapolis and 33-10 at Baltimore, are the most complete football of the season.

nextGame.headline: Rested Jaguars visit a 1-7 Titans team leaking short passes
nextGame.body:
Jacksonville is coming off 10 days of rest and is a 10.5-point favorite at Tennessee, with the moneyline at -550 and the total at 46.5. The Titans are 28th in net EPA and 27th on offense. Their defense is 26th against the pass and 30th on short throws, which plays straight into Lawrence's quick game and Parker Washington's role as the top target: Tennessee ranks 31st at holding WR1s to their usual output. Tennessee does get after the quarterback, with a pressure rate that ranks fourth. That is a real test for a line that's slow to release the ball and prone to flags. On the other side, Cam Ward's offense leans run and keeps the ball the least in the league, so a Jacksonville lead should turn Tennessee one-dimensional quickly.

Availability tilts further toward Jacksonville. The Jaguars' only listed absence is a safety inactive by coach's decision. Tennessee lists both starting-caliber linemen Peter Skoronski (hamstring) and JC Latham (finger) as questionable, behind a line that already ranks 30th in pressure rate allowed. Receiver Carnell Tate, running back Tyjae Spears, cornerback Jaylon Jones and the punter are out, and cornerback Marcus Harris is questionable. A thinner secondary and possibly a patched-up line are exactly what Jacksonville's pass rush and short-area defense feed on.

waysToWin.title: Live in the short passing game
waysToWin.body: Tennessee is 30th in EPA allowed on short throws and 29th in explosive pass rate allowed, and opposing WR1s have feasted. Lawrence can get the ball out quickly to Washington and Brenton Strange, which also blunts the Titans' pass rush. If the Titans can't tackle in space better than their 2nd-ranked missed-tackle rate suggests, this should be steady scoring.

waysToWin.title: Pressure a leaky, banged-up line
waysToWin.body: Tennessee's line allows the third-highest pressure rate, and two starters are questionable. Jacksonville's seventh-ranked pressure rate should force Ward into the hurried short throws this defense eats up. That is the recipe behind most of the 15 takeaways.

waysToWin.title: Get ahead and make them throw
waysToWin.body: The Titans pass well below expectation and own the league's lowest time of possession. Jacksonville's rush defense is third in EPA allowed. An early lead forces Tennessee off its preferred run-heavy script and into obvious passing downs.

waysToLose.title: Titans' pass rush wrecks drives
waysToLose.body: Tennessee's pressure rate is fourth in the league, and Jacksonville's line holds the ball longer than most and commits plenty of penalties. A few sacks plus flags could stall drives and keep a big underdog in the game. This is the most plausible way the spread, if not the game, slips away.

waysToLose.title: Ward hits the deep shots
waysToLose.body: Jacksonville is 27th in deep-pass EPA allowed. A couple of completions downfield from Ward would flip a game Tennessee can't win on long drives. Tate's absence makes that harder for the Titans, but one or two big plays is all an underdog needs.

waysToLose.title: Fourth-down aggression plus a turnover swing
waysToLose.body: Saleh's Titans have gone for it on every fourth down in reach. If those tries convert and Jacksonville's usual takeaways don't show up, the hidden points that power the Jaguars' margins disappear. Against Philadelphia, with no takeaways, Jacksonville won by just two.

nextGame.watch: How often Lawrence is hit when Tennessee's fourth-ranked pressure rate meets Jacksonville's slow-release, penalty-prone line. If he's clean, this gets lopsided.

restOfSeason.body:
The efficiency profile is the real thing, and it is better than last year's 13-win team that leaned on close-game luck. With a three-game lead over Houston and two games left against Tennessee and Indianapolis, the division should hold. What regresses is the turnover margin. Expect scoring to drift down from the current pace and points allowed to tick up as takeaways normalize, especially in the stretch against the Giants, Bears and Steelers.

The defense's deep-ball weakness is the matchup risk for January, and it showed against the two best passing attacks Jacksonville has seen. If the pass rush keeps winning early and the line trims its flags, this is a top-two seed in the AFC conversation. If not, it's still a comfortable playoff team.
swingFactors: How fast the takeaway rate regresses
Deep coverage against Chicago, New York and Pittsburgh
Offensive line penalties and pressure allowed

confidence.note: Eight-game sample and strong efficiency, but scoring is inflated by an unsustainable turnover margin.
